summary.text:
The balance sheet identity closes to the pound: CFR £1,392.08m less external borrowing £1,316.90m is exactly the £75.180m of internal borrowing they report. What that number means is the story — internal borrowing has been run down from a much higher level and the report says plainly that it now needs to be funded externally.

Two entirely different halves to a £1.3bn book. £404m matures twenty-five years or more out at a weighted 2.642%, and four £50m loans running to 2071 at under 2% carry about £119m of discount between them on today's curve. Above them £210.8m matures inside twelve months at 4.692%, and MUFG's recorded advice is to keep borrowing short until long rates improve — so the refinancing wall is rebuilt every year by design.

A fifth LOBO call for the library: £10m where the lender raised the rate above PWLB and Barnet exercised its option to repay.

officer.body:
Hi [OFFICER NAME],

Apologies for the cold email. PWLBtoday is fairly new so you may not have come across us yet.

We're built for local authority treasury teams and nothing else: live PWLB rates at both daily fixings, a monthly breakdown of every loan the sector draws, every council's PWLB book priced daily against the DMO's repayment curve, and a training academy for officers and members. There's more — the predictor, the SONIA path, peer metrics, a daily brief — in the brochure at [BROCHURE URL]. We don't sell treasury products, and the data side is free and stays free.

To keep that data and our training relevant we built tools that watch committee papers across every council in the country, so we can see how a council's own figures compare with where the market has gone since. So below are a few thoughts on the final outturn report that went to Finance and Growth Overview and Scrutiny on 20 July. You're not being singled out — every authority gets one of these — and there's no agenda in it.

A cross-check first. Your Fig 3 puts the CFR at £1,392.08m and Fig 7 puts external borrowing at £1,316.90m. The difference is £75.18m, which is exactly the internal borrowing figure you report in Fig 6. That closes to the pound, which is rarer than it should be and worth saying. We also hold 53 PWLB loans for Barnet totalling £1,297.7m, which sits comfortably inside the £1,316.90m once the MEEF and Green Finance Fund money is taken out.

What the shape of that book says is the reason we wrote. Splitting it by maturity: £404.3m matures twenty-five years or more out at a weighted 2.642%, and £210.8m matures inside twelve months at 4.692%. Two entirely different books wearing one name. Four £50m loans running to 2071 at 1.71%, 1.84%, 1.95% and 1.98% account for most of the long half.

On the DMO's premature repayment curve this afternoon, notice 314/26, those four alone price about £119.0m below par, and the whole book carries roughly £203.2m of discount against a balance of £1,290.9m. We're not suggesting anything follows from that — we don't sell treasury products, we model no MRP and no accounting treatment, and the DMO's quote is the only one that binds. Ours is indicative and the page says so. But it is the kind of number that is more useful seen daily than annually, and yours is at pwlbtoday.org/loan-analysis.

The short half is the live one. Your Fig 9 records MUFG advising that borrowing stay short "due to relatively high cost of long-term borrowing", with everything drawn in the year at up to two-year maturities and the portfolio to be restructured into longer-term loans once conditions improve. That is a defensible position and we've no view on it. What we'd note is only that it makes the £210.8m a recurring annual decision rather than a one-off, and the level it reprices at is not static: one-year certainty closed at 4.95% this afternoon and two-year at 5.06%, against the 4.692% the bucket currently carries. Our monthly sector breakdown at pwlbtoday.org/pwlb-activity is the other half of that — July was £368m across 33 loans from just 19 borrowers at an average 5.02%, so you can see how thin the market is before you need to be in it.

One smaller thing, because we've now seen it five times this summer. Your £10m of LOBOs where "lenders increased rates above PWLB" and the Council exercised its option to repay is the fifth call we've picked up in a few months — Kent, Tameside, Newcastle and York are the others, and the pattern across them is lenders testing the option now that PWLB rates have risen to meet them. That is a cross-council picture no single council can see from its own papers, and it is the sort of thing we publish.

On training, four fit Barnet. PWLB break costs — mechanics & live calculator is the engine above with the workings shown. PWLB repayment structures speaks to the annuity-versus-maturity split in the long half. LOBO loans (legacy) for the remaining options. And The Capital Financing Requirement (CFR) is written for members, which matters when internal borrowing has come down to £75.18m and the report says it "now needs to be funded by external borrowing". All 115 courses are free to local authorities until the end of September at pwlbtoday.org/academy, and free accounts for the whole team.

And if you do find it useful, mentioning it to others would help us more than anything. We're small, word of mouth is most of our marketing, and every sign-up helps us prove the need.

Sign up free → https://pwlbtoday.org/
Follow on LinkedIn → https://www.linkedin.com/company/pwlbtoday/

Russell
